title: 2026 08 27 Petitions
machineSummary: BARNZ and the Aviation Industry Association said they support a voluntary customer charter over regulation. The Commerce Commission said its Jetstar prosecution and Air New Zealand investigation target misleading delay information. MBIE said Pacific visa waiver decisions balance benefits against overstay risks, noting Tonga and Samoa statistics.

chunks.text: Thank you for patience. Now, our first submitter is from BARNZ, Board of Airline representatives. Ms O'Brien. Is she coming in on Zoom? I think Kath should be coming from Zoom. She's joined us on Zoom. Oh, here we go. All right. Ms. O'Brien, welcome. I'm Greg O'Connor.

I'm the chair of the Petitions Committee. I will just introduce ourselves for you. We've got the other submitters in the room, so we'll do our introductions now, and then we'll come back to you on the note. Andrew Bayly. Kia ora. Kia ora. Celia Wade-Brown. And joining you on Zoom is...

Kia ora, Kath. Greg Fleming, MP for Maungakiekie. All right. Kia ora. Great, that worked. All right. So now welcome, Kath. You've take your submissions as read, but we'd like to take us through the highlights, and you've got 10 minutes, so hopefully leave time for some questions. Welcome. Thank you so much. Thank you. And thank you for the opportunity to appear.

I know you have it, but for the record, my name is Kath O'Brien, and I am the executive director of the Board of Airline Representatives, which represents airlines flying to New Zealand. We have sort of 20 to 25 members at any one time, and that includes airlines that are international, in the majority, and also our domestic operators in New Zealand, Qantas, and airlines like Air Chathams.

I don't say that we represent every single airline, but we are the large majority. And so thank you for the opportunity to submit to this petition, and I will take the submission as read and will not go through every point. I think that the sort of key things that I would say is that there have been some substantial improvements by airlines post the pandemic recovery period in their operations, and in particular around their customer reaccommodation in the event of delay and cancellation. And I note the petition of Consumer New Zealand,

and I am sure that there are still scenarios where customer experiences are not what we would wish. And I think the Consumer New Zealand petition proposes a solution that isn't perfect in terms of using information disclosure regulation. An information disclosure is something that we use to monitor prices at regulated airports, or we use to monitor on-time performance of airlines as the Ministry of Transport publishes. And that regulation isn't particularly suitable for a solution for this problem.

But happily we do have a solution in train. And in my submission, I noted that there's work underway with the Aviation Council, of which BARNZ is a member, as are other members of the aviation system here in New Zealand. It is led by Minister James Shaw, and it is housed within the Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport.

So that council is working on a number of things to improve New Zealand's aviation system, and one of those is consumer information in the event of delays and cancellations and that sort of thing. And the Aviation Action Plan is publicly available, and the action relevant to that matter is in that action plan.

And the publicly available information tells us that officials have taken advice to Minister Shaw on this matter. And in fact, in very recent days, officials have been talking to airlines about a voluntary customer charter to address some of these challenges in a way that would improve outcomes for consumers.

And so we're quite a long way down the road on the work that would sort of put into a framework New Zealand's approach to this. And so I would just encourage the committee to seek advice from the Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport or indeed Minister Shaw, and allow that work to continue as it should, rather than adding another process that might be duplicitous on this matter.

Duplicitous, I don't think Yes. Duplicates anyway. So look, we have just been advised of that ourselves just before coming to this meeting, I might say, so that does sort of put something of a different dimension to where we're coming from. But thank you.

And I apologize, I know I called you BARNZ. You're not BARNZ because you're- There is a BARNZ, and they're really good at construction, I think. Yeah. But BARNZ is really good at flying planes, so Yes. And may never the twain meet. Indeed not. I don't think we can build a plane.

Yeah. So all right. Well, any questions, members for Ms. O'Brien. Can I ask you two questions, Kath? I'll come in. The first thing is the compensation that you get if you have a delay on an international flight under Montreal versus what you get paid out domestically, are they aligned?

Because often in airports you sort of get the $10 voucher, go and have a cup of coffee type stuff if you are delayed. What is the sort of level of compensation, and is that standard across the airlines? So the Montreal Convention is something that airlines have to comply with on their global networks and, of course, here in New Zealand.

And I don't profess to be an aviation lawyer, so I would not like to say exactly how it works. But I think here in New Zealand, and in line with the Montreal Convention, we talk about matters that are within and outside of the airline's control.

So if there is a weather event, for example, that is outside of the airline's control and generally does not attract, for example, compensation to the passenger. What airlines will do is they will re-accommodate that passenger on the next available service if they can and that sort of thing. And we've seen a lot of that, for example, when Auckland Airport flooded substantially, airlines worked really hard to re-accommodate those passengers even where they might not have had to. So I think airlines will go above sometimes what international conventions will otherwise dictate.

Okay. So the question of the timing, and you raise it twice in your report, and you do list them, there are clearly issues that the airline is responsible for. Yes. You don't have a crew turn up. You have an engine breakdown. Those you don't have to wait. And you talk about having to come to a firm view on where liability sits for a delay. Where it's evident and obvious that it is the airline, for instance, as opposed to someone on a ground handling service whacking into the side of the

plane. It happened in Wellington once with me. At that situation, do airlines automatically pay out and compensate and make people aware? Or that's where I think the way you wrote your report, it was very unclear about when there was clear liability and people were sitting in the airport as opposed to, oh, well, I don't know, if it's fog related or something like that, then that's a different issue, right?

Is it- I think that when the matter is within the airline's control, the most important thing that the airline is going to try and do immediately is actually get the customer where they wish to go. So they won't, for example, refund the customer and leave them stranded wherever they are and let them go off and buy a new ticket because that isn't getting the customer the service that they actually want, which is the travel.

So in the first instance, airlines will do all they can to get the customer where they need to go as soon as possible. And where that's not possible, and the delay or the disruption is within the airline's control, then that is something that airlines will give the customer options for refund or credit or travel on another service. Those other options then roll out. But the first thing is always, can we get the customer where they want to go?

All right. Thank you. All right. See you there. Greg Fleming, sorry. Well, kia ora ano. Kath, thank you for that. Just when I look at the Commerce Commission's investigation and ruling into Jetstar's challenges a couple of years ago, obviously they're pretty significant.

Do you have confidence that a voluntary charter is going to be adhered to? Look, I think actually it is the best and most pragmatic way that New Zealand could make quick progress to be clear about what it expects from its aviation system participants. I think one of the challenges that we've got at the moment is that there are a lot of complex frameworks emerging around the world, and they are generating very sort of perverse and unintended outcomes with a lot more delay and difficulty in

progressing complaints. And I think that actually if we wanted to have a sort of sensible run at this, having a voluntary charter is a great first step. And then if that is not working, then we can look at more difficult and frankly more costly solutions.

But actually, this is a really sensible first step. Okay. And I guess there's the make it clear to the airlines that what you just outlined is the process- Yeah. I think it will be important... which, again, is a pretty good incentive as well to follow the charter. Yeah, look, for sure. And I think it's really important to work with airlines, and indeed consumer groups to understand the concerns and make sure that what we do design meets the need.

And so it will be important to have a consultation process on this work, which we're not quite up to. And I guess my plea to this committee is to sort of allow for that process to continue because we are quite advanced and not add to another step somewhere else. Yeah. Susie White-Brown.

Thank you very much. Having experienced a recent two-day delay coming back to this country, one of the issues is the communication with the customer. It was not clear. If English hadn't been my first language, I don't think I would have had a clue what was going on, frankly.

The representative at the airport came and talked to small groups, different groups, different people in different queues. It was absolutely appalling. And in fact, being fairly sure of our rights as we tend to be in this- role. We did get our accommodation, and taxi, and food, and so on, all reimbursed very nicely and quickly. And presumably, we got on the first flight available.

But it was not clear as to whether people should be looking to rebook themselves or to... So all I'm saying is that the international regime is not particularly good for the customer either. So I think it's not only about the compensation, it's about who's making what efforts to get people rebooked.

I agree that airlines want to get you on the next flight. I think, yeah. It's just how the communication is done, as well as what the actual entitlements are, if we dare to use such a word in this house, would be helpful. Now, that was coming from overseas to here. I've not had great problems in this country.

But I would like to also think about if we start with this voluntary code of practice. In my view, a parallel process needs to be very clear as to whether it's being adhered to or not. Rather than us sitting, well, it won't be me, sitting here in five years' time saying, "Well, we had a voluntary code, and we don't really know how well it's worked."

Okay. I think, yeah. All right. Okay. I think a bit to go away, unless you want to reply to that, Kath. No, I would just, I guess, reflect the complexity of the international system, the challenges with local ground handlers in country. So for example, if a New Zealand carrier was flying overseas, they are likely to have a foreign company operating on the ground for them and explaining to their customers.

So more that airlines can do, as I know Air New Zealand has recently announced, to allow customers to self-serve some of that recovery themselves in the app and things like that. That's great, but I do acknowledge the international system is complex. There are many players, there are many ground handlers, and also we've got the challenge of travel agents who often make bookings and have their customer contacts, in effect, as the customer contact.

So when the airline reaches out to re-accommodate a customer- Mm... they bump into the travel agent. It is difficult, and we're constantly trying to improve that. It is one of the very greatest complexities of aviation. Absolutely. All right. Thank you for that. All right. Thank you. All right, thank you. You're welcome to remain on as we now have aviation industry.

Mr. Wallace, nice to see you again. Thank you, Mr. Chair. I'm probably going to sound very similar to Kath, but from a domestic perspective. Mm. Good. So look, I won't go through my submission, but we represent commercial aviation in New Zealand.

So Air New Zealand is a member of ours, but so are most of the regional airlines. But our membership encompasses the wider commercial aviation sector in New Zealand, so tourism flight operators, flight training schools, aviation engineers, agricultural aviation. So we cover what's known as general aviation, but the regional airlines and Air New Zealand are part of our membership.

I just want to acknowledge the concerns of Consumer New Zealand and their petition. I think a number of the concerns are valid, but as Kath has said, and I'm on the Aviation Council as well, as we speak, we have a process going through the Aviation Council that is looking at the rights of passengers, that is looking at the rights of consumers, and one of those things is a voluntary charter.

Now, I've talked to my members about a voluntary charter, so I've talked to Air New Zealand, I've talked to Air Chathams, I've talked to some of the other regional airlines. And frankly, it would be churlish if they weren't part of a voluntary charter, and they're prepared to sign up to a voluntary charter. Their only reticence is about something that imposes more costs.

So that's what we have to be very careful of in terms of the regional airlines. Mm. I think Consumer New Zealand in their presentation a few weeks ago said that the fuel crisis was something in control of airlines. It certainly is not. And many of our regional airlines are really, really struggling, as you know, and have rationalized routes, have cut routes.

And the last thing we want to do, frankly, is put more cost onto them through a change in the act, through a change in the Section 410 of the Civil Aviation Act, that would put more cost on them in terms of the regulatory burden they need to meet. So I guess what we're saying is, yeah, let's look at the voluntary charter.

We've got airlines that are prepared to sign up to it. We've got the process going through the Aviation Council now. And I'd like to think that whatever happens in the election, that the Aviation Action Plan will carry over to a new government, because everything in there is valid.

The other thing I wanted to say is that I talked with Air Chathams, who is one of our good members. And you were just talking before about some of the delays that passengers experience. And obviously weather is completely out of control of an airline, but things like engineering, staff not turning up, crew not turning up, that is the responsibility of the airline.

And in the case of Air Chathams, they do everything possible to support their passengers. A delay of more than 60 to 90 minutes, they're offering full refunds, whatever fare the passenger is on. They're offering refreshments. They're doing everything that's possible.

And that is easier if you're a smaller airline, I must say. So it is easier if you're a smaller airline to be able to do that. When you're Air New Zealand, it's not always obvious to a front desk staff member, or it's not always known to a front desk staff member what the cause of that delay is.

So therefore, the communication can't always be acknowledging that they're responsible for that delay. So those things do need to be taken into account. Recently you would have seen Air New Zealand have just last week actually introduced the APR, which is the automated passenger rebooking. Probably it's got more relevance to international because it will automatically rebook passengers for delays of more than four hours. So that is a system that they're now using.

And for pretty simple itineraries, the automatic passenger rebooking will be able to rebook passengers, the sort of things that you're talking about, Celie, with your delay. Mm. I think that's probably enough. I'm happy to answer hearts questions, but I guess I just want to say that we're acknowledging in the industry that this is a concern.

We're acknowledging Consumer New Zealand's petition, and there is a process underway to address that. All right. Questions, members. Celie. Yes. And you've just reminded me, I had a day's delay going to the Chathams. I was in the fortunate situation of having accommodation there.

It's not so much about the level of compensation. I think that's very important, don't get me wrong. But I think that's relatively clear in that if you're not booked on, and you need accommodation. Yes. It's really about the commitment in that chart. Have you talked in that charter or in the development of it about a commitment for clear communication and making sure that the customer has received that communication?

And again-... I think there are some complexities about if they've booked through a travel agent, for sure, and sometimes we have that ourselves with booking through parliamentary services. I understand that. But maybe they need to make sure that they do have the contact details direct for their passengers. I think there are some questions about that.

Yeah. Look, I don't have all the answers, Celie. That's the sort of stuff I haven't seen in the voluntary charter that's been drafted by the ministry. But communication is definitely a key part of that. And I think that whole area, all I can say is I think the whole area needs improvement. Mm-hmm. The other thing I'd say is that there is a Consumer Protections Act. You know about that- Mm-hmm... Andrew. And MB administers that.

Arguably, I think, and I put it in my submission- Mm... that is something that needs a lot more promotion. Because most of us wouldn't know to go there. And the rights of passengers are very clearly spelled out there. It needs the industry to promote it more, and it actually needs the government to promote it more. Mm.

All right. Any other questions, members? All right. I'll invite the Commerce Commission. Thank you. Table. Thanks, Tom. Very interesting. Thanks, you folks. Tena koutou. My name's Rebecca MacAtamney. I'm the acting chief executive of the Commerce Commission.

My substantive role is general manager in the Competition and Fair Trading branch. And I'm joined by my colleague Vicki Conlin who's a senior investigator in our fair trading team. So the commission's role in all of this is that we enforce the Fair Trading Act. So the Fair Trading Act, of course, doesn't require airlines to give any information to affected passengers.

But what it does require is that any information that is given is accurate and is not misleading. And as I think the committee knows, we have taken some action on that in recent years. We took some enforcement action against Jetstar, and we are currently investigating Air New Zealand for similar conduct. So we're really here in your hands to answer any questions you have. Unfortunately, I cannot give more information about the Air New Zealand investigation as it is still an active investigation.

However, I can say that we are on track to complete the investigation in September. All right. All right. Mr. Bailey. Thank you. Obviously ask you about the first question you posed. Mm-hmm. So the act doesn't require disclosure, which is clearly what this is about.

And then the second thing is you've taken enforcement actions about making sure it's not misleading. But the first issue, the more central issue, and it's what my good colleague's been talking about. So I'm asking from the perspective of the Commerce Commission, do you believe that there should be a requirement for disclosure in the act under the consumer trading? And I'll give you another analogy, is that if you buy toys for children, they normally have instructions.

So do you have a view that there should be a change, a legislative change, or? As a general rule, the commission supports any initiative that is going to end up with consumers having more and better information so they understand their rights and can use that information to enforce those rights.

Whether that is through a change to the legislation or not is probably a question for M sert. Okay. So the next question is, you've obviously taken two prosecution cases around misleading issue. Has your investigation looked at whether in fact- Under the disclosure that the airlines had made, were in fact they complied with their own rules around granting people the issue like a coffee, whatever. We heard from Mr. Wallace just before.

Has it gone to that second step? I'll ask Becky to comment on that. Thank you. Obviously, the Jetstar investigation has been completed and has gone to prosecution, whereas the Air New Zealand investigation is still underway. But both of them, we are looking at potential misrepresentations of the information that they have already provided to people. So both Air New Zealand and Jetstar already- Sorry, with all due respect, that's not quite the nuanced question I was asking. I understand that bit, but my question, sorry, probably my fault,

is when you were looking at prosecution of those two parties, potential whatever, did you score and did you go and source what the airlines had said that they would do in a situation where there was a delay? And then looked at that and said, well, have they been meeting that requirement of their disclosed things that they would do in the event of delay or whatever.

Did they actually deliver the coffee or whatever? Yeah, that's right. In the Jetstar investigation, we discovered that Jetstar were not always honoring what they stated publicly that they would do. So there's two issues. With Jetstar, they were providing information to passengers that was not completely in compliance with what passengers' rights actually were under the Civil Aviation Act and the Montreal Convention. And then secondly, there were also instances where when people actually made claims to Jetstar to get reimbursement of the costs that

they had incurred, whether that be the cost of an alternative flight with Air New Zealand, if Jetstar weren't able to rebook them adequately or the cost of a hotel. Jetstar were making misleading representations around particularly the amounts that people could claim for things like hotels, which went against their stated information.

All right. Of course, you answered the question. Just one last observation from you. You're obviously looking at both airlines, major airlines. The observation I was going to ask you, did you see a similarity around the extent of what compensation both airlines would offer in event of default? Because the reason I'm asking this question is that it's been proposed it's this voluntary code, which hopefully might standardize the response.

But I'm just trying to ask you, in your investigation, did it become obvious that some airlines, they had a different level of compensation to the others, or was it reasonably standard? It's reasonably standard because it's governed by the Civil Aviation Act and the Montreal Convention. Both of those set out statutory limits for the amounts that the airlines are liable for.

I guess with Air New Zealand, because the fare tickets are often higher, the overall level would be higher because it's linked to the cost of the ticket being 10 times for domestic fares. But the policies themselves largely reflect what consumers should be entitled to in law. So it's just reimbursement of costs that they have incurred up to those statutory limits.

The main issues that we've seen is when people actually try to claim those costs, how those costs are being assessed by the airlines and subsequently paid to consumers, and the explanations they're being given for the amounts that are being offered to them. Okay. Thank you. All right. Thank you. And Mr. Fleming, you've got a question. Yes. Yeah, tena koutou. I appreciate the question I'm about to ask will be a difficult one for you guys to answer.

So I'll try and phrase it in a way where you might be able to. I just I know that this is a question that the petitioner would want me to ask. Given the behavior that you have seen from the two airlines, in particular, obviously, Qantas with the prosecution already so far. The deliberation that we as a committee are considering as to whether we recommend a voluntary code or a mandated one, do you have any advice for us as to extra things that we might consider in deciding whether we're being realistic in landing on a voluntary code as being

effective? I think that both of those are initiatives that will lead to consumers having greater levels of information. So they're both positive outcomes. Obviously, with regulation, you've got more certainty for consumers. However, you also have more cost, both for the airlines and for the regulator, whoever that might end up being.

Right. Thank you. All right. Look, thank you very much. What we do now, having heard from the different parties, we'll prepare a report and recommendation, obviously taking into account the minister's letter, which we only got this afternoon ourselves. So thank you very much.

Thank you. And to our online. Right. So we now come to next item. We've got the ministry, MB. You like to be referred to as MB or prefer the full name of Business- MB's fine Innovation and Employment. All right. Thank you. I think you were here.

I'm sure if you were here we introduced Greg O'Connor, the chair of the committee. Andrew Beynon. Yeah. Jenny-May Brown. And online. Greg Fleming She was still upright. It's good. Yeah. Shall we, we can introduce ourselves if you like. Get a bit of group here. So, kia ora koutou. My name's Sian Roguski.

I'm the General Manager, Employment Skills and Immigration Policy, joined here with Jock Gilray, who's our Deputy Chief Operating Officer for Immigration New Zealand. I've got Steve Watson, who's General Manager, Immigration Compliance- Hi... and Investigations. And Sam Foley, who's Manager of the International and Humanitarian Immigration Policy team.

I think you've got- We've all come a long way, haven't we, Steve? So cops in the Wairarapa. So thank you for the opportunity to submit, and provide some evidence. We didn't necessarily think we would kind of open up with any particular remarks. I think you've got the information there, and just to maximize time for questions.

But what I thought I would mention, because I realized we didn't relay this to the clerk of the committee. Depending on where some of your questions get to, for example, if it starts to get into risk settings or perhaps some kind of international relations, they may be some questions that we'd be happy to answer, but they may be best for a closed session.

So, we'll let you know if it just happens to get there. All right. So- All right. So one of the central questions, and I'm going off memory a little bit, is the assertion that Pacific Islanders don't pose a higher risk than necessarily other populations. And therefore, I think, the conclusion is that it seems manifestly unfair.

How would you respond to that specific assertion? Yeah. Well, maybe I might just start just talking a little bit about the general framework that we've set out in the paper around... Because the core question I think that's raised by the petitioner is cabinet consideration of whether visa-free status should be- Yeah... extended. And as I think as we mentioned, any advice that is invited from the Minister of Immigration or other members of Cabinet and that's put forward is around a framework that sort of dates from about 2015. And as you

mentioned, it has both a kind of risk part of the ledger and a benefits part of the ledger. Like you say, the risk of overstaying is one particular element what's on the risk side, but there's also other things that we'd be looking at as well, regardless of the country that, or, you know, that we're looking at.

So that includes national security, passport security, general integrity of the immigration system, what the impact there is. The external push factors from that particular country, health and biosecurity. And then on the benefit side of the ledger, we'd absolutely be looking and advising on the international relationships at play, trade opportunities, and tourism growth.

So we absolutely sort of recognize that, in this particular petition, that the issue has been raised about is the government treating Pacific countries differently. That sort of sits within a wider holistic framework, if you like, of any country that would sort of be put forward.

Okay. That doesn't help me much in terms of answering the question. So I assume, on the benefits side- Mm... Pacific Islanders play an important role in New Zealand. So, the question probably turns on risk assessment and so when you are doing the risk assessment, presumably MBIE does that on your behalf and informs the minister.

So what I'm trying to understand, because whether the petitioner's right or wrong, I don't know. I'm trying to get an... It's an open question to them. Mm. That's why it's quite a direct open question. Yeah. And I'm trying to understand why is that assertion, because it seems to be because it's hard, it must be that assertion.

So going back to that very definite question they asked. Do Pacific Islanders, are they deemed to be a higher risk category than perhaps if you come from Germany or America or Britain or China? Yeah. Why don't you talk to stats? So one of the ways that we would look at that is through the annual estimate of overstayers or the unlawful estimate, and I have got last year's figures. And I think, if I remember rightly, Greg Fleming raised when the petition was raised about the top 10 countries. But there is a second table that

compares the percentages against arrivals. And Tonga and Samoa are the top two in terms of the percentage of arrivals who remain unlawfully in New Zealand. So that would be one thing that we would look at in terms of a risk profile. So just so what timeframe is that?

That was those arrivals since July 2023 to 30th of June 2025. Right. And so those two groups represent... Just could you say that again? That- So we produce a- Yeah... top 10 of numbers. But then you've got to dig deeper into the data and put those numbers as a percentage of arrivals.

And Tonga and Samoa and Fiji are in the top four. Malaysia's third. So that is one of the factors that we would use in determining the risk settings. Just to sup on that. I understand the maths, but why does that increase the risk? I mean, surely it's the total numbers that impact, if they do, that impact health, education, those issues that you mentioned. So why do you say that it's the percentage that matters rather than the crude numbers?

That's a good question. But- So we're basing it on country by country Yeah. By country. Yeah. Every single country is based on- I understand that... a likely pool of risk of the nationalities of that country-... potentially overstaying. So the higher potential rate of overstaying is a higher potential for those countries.

So when we look at other countries which have a lower rate of overstaying, a bit less risk overall, although they might have the high numbers of people arriving. Hmm. I still don't understand why you are concerned about the percentages of arrivals than the actual numbers. We're concerned about both. About both, yeah. And there are other policy factors that are taken into consideration in advising the minister.

Question then. Let's just make up a country. Nirvana is a country- Oh, no.... that all of a sudden we have a spike of people coming from Nirvana that the statistics started to, which do currently have the visa waiver. Hmm. What would trigger them to have to be then treated in a similar manner?

Cabinet- I mean, I think again that comes back where there is sort of consistent and continually monitoring of the immigration system and exactly where we're seeing some of those risks come through. If in our case, Nirvana, was showing this kind of enhanced risk, that would be something that we would be raising with ministers. Again, any assessment, for example, of removal of visa waiver status goes through exactly that same sort of framework that I outlined.

And I think the last time that advice was tendered and Cabinet made decisions on that dates back to South Africa, which was 2016 or '15. Yeah, 2016 they were removed from visa. Yeah. Now obviously- South Africa were removed from- Correct. Yeah. Have they been reinstated? No, they haven't. And you can imagine, and this is why it's a Cabinet decision. It's quite a decision to go forward and extend a visa waiver.

It's a heck of a decision to, because again, it plays into those international relations to rescind and take back a visa waiver status is also obviously a significant sort of cross-Cabinet decision as well. Okay. Let's- Great. Oh, sorry, Mr. Fleming. Hmm. Yeah, thank you. You said in your written submission that the visa waiver was put in place some 25, 30 years ago, I think.

But after just a few days it was withdrawn because of concerns around overstaying. I mean, essentially, what we've got here is an issue of, it's a lack of trust, isn't it, from New Zealand to those Pacific countries. That if we extend the visa waiver, we're going to have significant problems with overstaying.

The petitioner's argument to that is that the overstaying at the moment is a result of the fact that it's so difficult to get into the country. So it's essentially a chicken and the egg. Do you have any comments to that regard? I mean, I appreciate this is probably outside of your gamut in terms of what you're able to speak to. But the more I've looked at this issue, the more considered it both beforehand and through this process, it seems to me that one side needs to take the first step somehow in terms of restoring that trust.

I mean, I guess what I would comment is that the visa waiver policy does sort of sit within a wider suite of policy options that ministers have asked for and looked for. And I think what we touched upon in the submission is, short of visa waiver, what are the other things that we can do to kind of take a step forward towards that space. So that includes the two-year multi-entry visa that was sort of relatively recently extended, the reduction in fees, the sort of escalated processing in times of urgency, so through funerals.

I absolutely appreciate the petitioner's views of, well, that doesn't go the full distance, but I think it kind of reflects that these are sort of potential steps. I mean, more broadly, right across government, I think agencies have relationships and work that they're doing with Pacific counterparts to absolutely address what are the ways that we can kind of move forward and address some of the risks that might- Hmm... prevent you from going forward.

So that's probably- Okay. I appreciate that. Can I just ask a follow-up question then? Because again, you say in your written report you talk about the fact that even quite... Or, no, it wasn't in there, or it might have been in your introductory remarks today. You talk about the fact that even as of last year, there's been concerns around compliance for those that are coming in. What would be, within your experience, for both these countries and all countries, how long would you need to see compliance by a country
